Addison Times Student Podcast: Episode 2
Panelists Emma Claxton, Hannah Baker, Chloe Caldwell and Naomi Garringer discuss the bell-to-bell student phone ban that has passed the Indiana House and Senate. Senate Bill 78 builds on an existing ban on cell phones in Indiana classrooms during instructional time, which is largely left up to teacher discretion, The Indianapolis Star reported. The new legislation would make the ban effective during the entire school day, and it would be up to schools to decide how to store devices to make them inaccessible to students.
GAME FACE
Shelbyville High School junior Kieran O’Connor paints a student’s face during Tuesday’s basketball game. O’Connor was one of several members of the school’s National Art Honor Society offering free face-painting, with bear paws emerging as the most popular design. A handful of younger fans opted instead for the jersey numbers of their favorite Golden Bears. | photo by ARELI CADENA-MORENO
County Plan Commission Issues Annual Report
Despite reviewing more zoning and development petitions than the year before, the Shelby County Plan Commission reported its lowest permit activity in a decade in 2025. The steady decline from the 2021 peak is likely related to affordability concerns and the county’s more cautious approach to commercial growth, the Plan Commission’s annual report said. While operating costs fell enough to offset much of the lost permit revenue, new home construction remained largely consistent with long-term averages, aside from the post-pandemic surge.
The total value of construction in the county last year was $24.7 million, down from $31 million in 2024. The value of improvements in 2024 was $327.1 million, though the majority of that total was due to the Speedway Solar project. Below is a graph from the report showing total value of improvements going back to 2015.
The county issued 31 new home permits last year, with new home development occurring primarily in the northwest quadrant of the county. The median home value of new homes last year was $345,000, about $50,000 higher than the median home value in 2023 and 2024.

NOTEBOOK:
Prologis will host a community meeting Wednesday, March 11, to share information about Project Hackman, a proposed data center development in Shelbyville. The open-house session will run from 5 to 8 p.m. at Shelbyville High School, 2003 S. Miller St. Project team members will be available throughout the evening to answer questions and discuss details of the proposal.
City Attorney Jenny Meltzer is stepping down after eight years in the role, Mayor Scott Furgeson confirmed. The city contracts with McNeely Law for legal services, and the firm will assign another attorney to assume responsibility for city matters.
Police were dispatched to First Financial Bank on Marketplace Blvd. after a motorhome struck a properly parked vehicle in the parking lot. The driver told officers he was attempting to park across multiple spaces while operating a 31-foot motorhome when the rear of his vehicle hit the parked car. He was cited for driving without a valid license, and officers also noted a broken taillight on the motorhome. The parked vehicle sustained damage to its driver-side rear bumper.
The Shelbyville High School Tree Trot 5K Run/Walk will take place Saturday, April 18, at Blue River Memorial Park. Registration opens at 7 a.m., and the race begins at 8 a.m. Proceeds will support tree planting along the Blue River, and age-group winners will receive handmade medals and saplings; early registration discounts are available through April 4.

HOOSIER NEWS: Construction is underway on a new 60,000-square-foot headquarters for West Side Tractor just off I-74 and Post Road in Indianapolis. The 20-acre site will house a showroom for John Deere equipment, demonstration spaces and expanded rental inventory, and will nearly triple the company’s current Indiana footprint as it continues to grow its presence statewide. This Day in Shelby County History
Local headlines reported on or around this date in Shelby County history. Selections are curated by The Addison Times from Shelby County Public Library Genealogy Department materials.
2006: A bill introduced by State Rep. Luke Messer aimed at reducing high school dropouts was drawing national attention, with Time magazine and Oprah Winfrey expressing interest in visiting Shelby County to cover the story. Messer noted that while most Indiana high schools reported graduation rates in the 90s, students who dropped out between school years were excluded, putting the true rate closer to 70%.
1996: Junne Barnett, interim director of the Grover Museum, discovered a cowhide-covered trunk while retrieving Civil War artifacts from storage. The collection included a battle-worn canteen, saber and scabbard, and other memorabilia; the trunk had been donated years earlier by a granddaughter of railroad pioneer William Peaslee.
1986: Shelbyville High School’s Shelly Caplinger was named one of Indiana’s top 40 senior girls’ basketball players and was invited to a workout scrimmage for the Indiana Girls All-Stars. Caplinger hoped to become the third Shelbyville girl to play in the Indiana’s annual All-Star series with Kentucky. Brenda Kelsay was an All-Star in 1981, and Teri Staker, who played three seasons at Shelbyville before transferring to Columbus North, was an All-Star in 1983.
1976: Janell Beth Hilton, Morristown, was named the 1976 Purdue Agricultural Queen at the annual Agriculture Awards Banquet. Hilton was a sophomore majoring in agricultural communication and education.
The Shelby County Plan Commission approved the Knighthood Manor subdivision, which would contain 15 lots over 10 acres on Knightstown Road.
1966: One of the last remaining landmarks from the era when Shelbyville was a major furniture manufacturing center was demolished. The former Blanchard-Hamilton Furniture Co. building, located at the southeast corner of South Noble and South streets, was constructed near the turn of the century and operated until 1950. Owned by Henry Joseph, the structure later housed Albert Furniture Co. and was eventually used as a PPG Industries warehouse.
1956: Officials with Kroger announced the local store would be closed until further notice due to significant storm damage. Remodeling was expected to begin soon.
1946: Thomas Fischer, 12, was among 35 county agriculturists honored at the annual farm recognition ceremony hosted by the Lions Club. A sixth-grade student at St. Vincent School, Fischer received the Indiana Corn Prince award for the second consecutive year.
1936: County officials asked that no heavy traffic be on county roads. The ground was frozen to a depth of 40 inches in various places, and the sudden thaw had softened road surfaces. Even roads surfaced with tarvia were having issues, they said.
1926: Work began on a three-story brick-and-steel building on East Washington Street, across from the Big Four Railroad tracks, for a new H.H. Walker Wholesale Grocery Co. store.
1916: The tabernacle building on West Broadway was sold to William Spiegel, who planned to reuse the lumber to build barns on his farm properties.
